headline: High-risk shared workspace and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Semantic Kernel can use MCP servers and application-defined files, while EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from EMQX-fed workflows can reach SK tool prompts or plugin inputs. The pair lacks explicit provenance controls, so the interaction is inferred rather than directly documented.
conditions: IF EMQX-fed content is passed into Semantic Kernel prompts or MCP tools without sanitization
IF a shared file or message queue is used as the bridge between the two agents
mitigations: Add a strict allowlist for fields forwarded from EMQX to Semantic Kernel
Insert a provenance tag and reject untrusted tool instructions
Disable MCP tools for any untrusted EMQX-derived payloads
Use a separate workspace directory for each agent
requires-engineering: add content-signature verification before tool execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Semantic Kernel touches application context and can send data to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face/MCP servers. If the pair shares files or context, sensitive IoT or application data can flow from one agent into the other and then out to third-party services. The profiles do not show isolation, so the leakage path is plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF EMQX outputs are stored in files or context that Semantic Kernel reads
IF Semantic Kernel forwards that context to a model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Keep IoT data and agent context in separate directories
Redact secrets before handing EMQX output to Semantic Kernel
Turn off automatic file ingestion in Semantic Kernel workflows
Restrict outbound destinations to approved endpoints only
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on all inter-agent transfers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX has broad network egress and HTTP API access, while Semantic Kernel can write files, read files, and use MCP servers. Even without shell or git writes, both can mutate shared application state through files or remote APIs, so concurrent updates can collide. The concurrency model mentions shared state via memory store, which increases conflict likelihood.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or memory store
IF EMQX API actions and Semantic Kernel plugin calls target the same mutable resource
mitigations: Assign separate writable directories to each agent
Use per-resource locks around shared memory-store writes
Serialize plugin calls that mutate the same backend
Add optimistic concurrency checks on shared records
requires-engineering: introduce a coordinator for cross-agent write arbitration

D_cascading_error.rationale: Semantic Kernel is a multi-agent orchestration layer that can act on plugin outputs, while EMQX can emit network-facing data through HTTP APIs and broad egress. If EMQX output is treated as authoritative by Semantic Kernel, errors can cascade into downstream tool calls or agent actions. Because no verification step is documented, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF Semantic Kernel uses EMQX output as input to a plugin or agent action without validation
IF downstream actions are triggered from EMQX-derived facts
mitigations: Require schema validation before Semantic Kernel consumes EMQX output
Add a human approval step for any downstream action
Log and compare EMQX outputs against a second source
Mark EMQX data as untrusted in prompts and tool metadata
requires-engineering: implement verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Semantic Kernel handles application context and may send data to Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Hugging Face, or MCP servers. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or DPA controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the data classes differ and the pair can move data across third-party services, medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF IoT data from EMQX includes regulated personal data
IF Semantic Kernel routes that data to a third-party model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Classify IoT payloads before forwarding them
Block regulated data from third-party model calls
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Restrict model providers to approved compliance regions
requires-engineering: add residency and DPA enforcement checks
